title: Kumarajiva
hook: the translator who put the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti into Chinese that people still read
tomorrow: The tongue that did not burn

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ming's dream, and the legend of sutras carried into Luoyang on a horse's back. Your line was carried in. What did someone carry into your life? Today, the end of the week, and a translator whose Chinese is still read aloud. Day nine hundred three.

All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, like lightning. That is the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra as it is chanted in Chinese in East Asian temples. The Chinese they chant comes from a translation made in Chang'an, by a team gathered around one monk born in an oasis town on the Silk Road. Quick pictures, each one gone almost as soon as it appears, set down in a Chinese that still sounds clear. His name was Kumarajiva.
screen: `A DREAM, A BUBBLE, DEW, LIGHTNING.` → `CHANTED IN CHINESE.` → `ONE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: First, where he came from. His biography says he was born in Kucha, one of those oasis towns, to a mother from the royal family and a father from India. He became a monk as a boy and studied in Kashmir. He knew the texts, and he came to know Chinese. Second, the long wait. When a Chinese army took Kucha, Kumarajiva was carried off by a general and held for years in a frontier town. It was there, some readers think, that his Chinese grew strong. Third, the work. A later ruler brought him to the capital, Chang'an, and gave him a large team of monks and scholars. Kumarajiva would hold the text, speak it in Chinese, discuss the hard words with the team, and the scribes would write. From that room came the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra in the versions still chanted and studied. Fourth, his way of translating. His biography tells a story: he said that turning Sanskrit into Chinese is like chewing rice before feeding it to someone. The flavor is lost, and the food may even turn the stomach. He knew what translation costs. Even so, his versions read as clear, flowing Chinese that people could actually say aloud, and some readers credit that clarity for how long they have lasted. Look back at this week: old texts read again, a southern road, a teaching that traveled, monks with merchants, translators at a table, a white horse. And now the translator whose words people still say.
screen: `BORN IN KUCHA.` · `HELD FOR YEARS ON THE FRONTIER.` · `A TEAM IN CHANG'AN.` · `CHEWED RICE: WHAT IS LOST.` · then, large: `THE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one well-made sentence. Take the line from the hook: all conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, like lightning. Say it aloud once, giving each picture its own pause. Notice how each picture is short, and how each one passes. Then settle with the breath. Let each out-breath be one of the six images: a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, lightning. Let it go, and start again. The bell holds the time.
Kumarajiva. The monk from Kucha whose Chinese translations of the Lotus, the Diamond and the Vimalakirti Sutras are still read and chanted. Today's word.
Your line: the translator. Today, when you explain something to someone, choose the clear sentence over the clever one, and see if it lands. Day nine hundred three.

howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese temples, Kumarajiva's versions of the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra are chanted in services and studied in classes.

fork.setup: you're Kumarajiva. a phrase in the Sanskrit is exact but would sound clumsy in Chinese. what do you do?
options: keep it word for word, however it sounds.
make it clear Chinese that people can read, even if some flavor is lost.
fork.reveal: his versions read as clear, readable Chinese. his chewed-rice saying admits what is lost, and his versions are the ones people still chant.

original.note: Sanskrit form of the translator's name, Kumārajīva.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kumarajiva was a famous old monk.
what it means: he was the translator whose Chinese versions of the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti Sutras are still read.
what a scholar hears: his teams' Chinese leans toward readability over literalness, and his versions stayed in use even where later, more literal translations were made.

notes: Diamond Sutra closing verse paraphrased from Kumarajiva's Chinese (dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning); Max Müller's 1894 SBE translation from Sanskrit has a different list and was not quoted.
Hook phrased as chanted in East Asian temples, avoiding a count of chanters.
Biographical details (Kucha, royal mother, Indian father, Kashmir study, captivity by a general, invitation to Chang'an) from the Gaoseng zhuan; no dates or team size given under the claims rule.
The chewed-rice saying is attributed to his biography; confirm attribution.
'Some readers think his Chinese grew strong in captivity' is a scholarly suggestion; confirm.

Editor pass: the chewed-rice saying corrected (the biography says the flavor is lost and it can even cause nausea; 'the nourishment is there' was not in it) and no longer framed as his stated reason for choosing clear Chinese; 'that choice is why his versions lasted' softened to 'some readers credit that clarity'; hook no longer says 'one man's translation, not a committee', which contradicted the team in the teach; match, myth, fork reveal and trapdoor aligned; practice wording varied from day 897's.
